title: Serbia's direct lignite subsidies rival the support renewables would need
programme: Direct subsidies to lignite electricity producers
problem: Serbia's ageing, inefficient lignite plants depend on government subsidies to keep operating.
solution: The state pays direct subsidies to lignite electricity producers; the study compares these with the support renewables would need to replace lignite.
funding: Public money paid as direct subsidies to coal and lignite electricity production.
results: Direct lignite subsidies reached 41.36 million EUR in Serbia in 2019, against 22.71 million EUR in Bosnia and Herzegovina and 6.59 million EUR in Kosovo. The study finds the support renewables would need to replace lignite is of a comparable size.
serbia_reason: Serbia paid the region's largest direct lignite subsidies in 2019, supporting the lignite generation of its state-owned utility EPS. Redirecting this money is a ready funding lever for renewables.
adapt_needed: Subsidy flows to lignite generation would need to be made transparent and gradually shifted into renewable support schemes.
blockers: Subsidies protect mining jobs and low power prices, so cutting them is politically sensitive.
quote: The financial RES support needs are comparable to current estimates of direct subsidies provided to lignite electricity producers. In 2019, the lignite subsidies amounted to 22.71 million EUR in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 6.59 million EUR in Kosovo and 41.36 million EUR in Serbia (Miljevic, 2020).

title: Serbia's planned Kostolac B3 and Kolubara B1 lignite units risk losses
programme: Kostolac B3 and Kolubara B1 new lignite units
problem: Serbia is adding new lignite capacity while carbon pricing and the EU carbon border adjustment threaten lignite revenues.
solution: Serbia is pursuing two new lignite units, Kostolac B3 (at an advanced stage) and Kolubara B1, part of about 2 GW of new lignite planned in the region.
implementer: Electric Power Industry of Serbia (EPS) and the Government of Serbia
funding: The study says the region's planned lignite units rely on Chinese or unclear financing.
results: Both Serbian projects have a positive net present value only without carbon pricing; a carbon border adjustment worsens their economics and an ETS phase-in makes all planned lignite units unprofitable. The 2 GW planned in the region would, if built, generate a cumulative loss by 2040.
serbia_reason: These are Serbia's own new lignite investments by its state utility EPS. Their value hinges on CBAM and on carbon pricing adopted through the Energy Community.
adapt_needed: Remaining spending decisions would need to be re-tested against CBAM and ETS carbon prices, plant by plant.
blockers: Kostolac B3 is already at an advanced stage, so sunk costs and contracts push towards completing it.
quote: With a CBA, the economic situation for plants gets worse; if the ETS is phased in, all planned lignite power plants turn net negative and hence are unprofitable. Consequently, any form of carbon pricing (at the border via a CBA or through an ETS phase-in) poses a major risk for the economics of new lignite plants in the region.

title: Bosnia's planned Kakanj 8 and Gacko 2 units unprofitable in every scenario
programme: Kakanj G8 and Gacko 2 new lignite units
problem: Bosnia and Herzegovina plans new lignite units although its mines are small and among the most cost-intensive in the region.
solution: National plans include new lignite units Kakanj G8 and Gacko 2 as part of the roughly 2 GW of new lignite planned in the region.
implementer: Bosnia and Herzegovina governments and power utilities (project sponsors)
funding: The study says the region's planned lignite units rely on Chinese or unclear financing.
results: The study's net present value analysis finds Kakanj G8 and Gacko 2 loss-making in all scenarios, even without carbon pricing. It attributes losses to low mining efficiency, air pollution compliance costs and limited exports under the EU carbon border adjustment.
serbia_reason: Serbia's new lignite faces the same Energy Community pollution rules and CBAM exposure on exports. A neighbour's projects failing even before carbon pricing shows the risk of locking in new lignite.
adapt_needed: Serbia's cheaper mines change the numbers, so the same test would need to be run with Serbian plant and mine cost data.
blockers: The projects remain in national strategies and political support for lignite jobs is strong.
quote: Figure 56 illustrates the results of the economic assessment of the proposed lignite projects in the region. Notably, Kakanj G8 and Gacko 2 have a negative NPV in all scenarios.

title: Energy Community pollution limits breached, forcing refurbish-or-close decisions by 2028
programme: Energy Community Large Combustion Plants Directive (NERP and opt-out derogations)
problem: Western Balkan lignite plants, including Serbia's ageing 4 GW fleet, emit far more SO2, NOx and dust than the applicable limits allow.
solution: The Energy Community Treaty adopted EU large combustion plant limits with three routes: a National Emission Reduction Plan (NERP), an opt-out with 20,000 operating hours, or direct compliance. Together they set 2028 as the deadline for plant-level compliance with stricter EU IED limits.
implementer: Energy Community and national governments of the Contracting Parties
results: Nearly all units exceeded their 2018 limits, with Kakanj in Bosnia and Herzegovina emitting 17 times its SO2 ceiling, and most opted-out units had already used more than their share of operating hours in 2018. The plants' pollution is linked to up to 3,000 premature deaths a year in the region.
serbia_reason: Serbia is bound by these Energy Community obligations, which make 2028 the plant-level compliance deadline. Every Serbian lignite unit expected to run beyond 2028 needs a refurbish-or-close decision now.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need a unit-by-unit plan that matches refurbishment spending to each unit's expected remaining operating years.
blockers: Refurbishing old units is costly and weak enforcement has so far allowed limits to be exceeded.
quote: Combined, they effectively imply a 2028 final deadline for plant-level compliance with the newer and stricter EU IED via LCP BREF limits. Considering the poor compliance performance of the operational fleet today, any compliant operation beyond 2028 will require significant refurbishment and investment.

title: Serbia's lignite-centred energy plans exposed to carbon pricing costs
programme: Energy Sector Development Strategy of the Republic of Serbia to 2025 (projections to 2030)
problem: Serbia's current plans keep lignite central through retrofits and new units, with only slow growth of renewables.
solution: Continuing current national energy planning: modernising existing lignite units to extend their lifetimes and meet pollution rules, building planned new units and expanding renewables slowly.
implementer: Ministry of Mining and Energy of Serbia
results: With an ETS phase-in, the study finds a renewables-led path cuts Serbia's cumulative generation costs by over 30 bn € compared with current plans. Under current plans, Serbia's investment of 8.9 bn € by 2050 is concentrated on lignite and gas.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own strategy, and its main risk comes from CBAM and possible ETS alignment under the Energy Community. Keeping lignite central would pass rising carbon costs to consumers.
adapt_needed: The national strategy would need to be stress-tested against CBAM and ETS carbon prices before further lignite investment.
blockers: Serbia's lignite is the cheapest in the region, which makes the fossil path look affordable until carbon pricing applies.
quote: The current Fossil strategy is, therefore, very vulnerable to a future phase-in of ETS, which would result in sharply rising generation costs and increasing consumer prices.

title: Financial de-risking cuts Serbian onshore wind costs by a fifth
programme: Western Balkans Guarantee Facility (Western Balkans Investment Framework)
problem: A high cost of capital in South East Europe (around 12 per cent) makes renewable projects far more expensive to finance than in Germany.
solution: The EU is offering budget guarantees to de-risk renewable investment, including a Western Balkans Guarantee Facility under the Western Balkans Investment Framework, part of the Economic and Investment Plan.
funding: EU budget guarantees; the Economic and Investment Plan aims to mobilise up to EUR 9 billion of IPA III grants for the region in 2021-2027.
results: Cited analysis finds financial de-risking lowers the levelised cost of onshore wind in Serbia by 20 per cent. Cutting the cost of capital from 12 to 3.5 per cent would let twice as much onshore wind be built with the same capital.
serbia_reason: Serbia can draw on WBIF and IPA III guarantees to cut the financing cost of wind and solar. The study presents low-cost renewables as the realistic replacement for its old lignite plants.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need bankable auction or contract schemes so that guarantees can be attached to individual projects.
blockers: Permitting, grid access and investor risk perceptions may limit how much guarantees lower costs.
quote: Low cost renewable energy projects are thus a real alternative for replacing old and polluting lignite power plants. As shown elsewhere, financial derisking have a considerable impact on RES financing costs, for example lowering the LCOE of onshore wind projects in Serbia by 20 per cent.

title: Kosovo C lignite plant repeatedly abandoned but kept in national plans
programme: Kosovo C (Kosova e Re) lignite power plant
problem: Kosovo relies almost exclusively on lignite from units older than 30 years.
solution: The government has kept the new Kosovo C lignite plant in national plans as a political priority despite the project being repeatedly abandoned.
funding: Financing has not been secured; the study cites well-founded doubts that it can be re-secured.
results: The study doubts the project can re-secure financing; its net present value is positive only without carbon pricing and turns negative if an ETS is phased in.
serbia_reason: Like Serbia, Kosovo is an Energy Community party whose new lignite would face the EU CBAM on exports. It shows how a politically favoured coal project can stall for years once financing falls away.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to confirm that any planned lignite unit has secure, carbon-price-tested financing before committing public resources.
blockers: Political attachment to lignite as a domestic resource keeps such projects in national plans.
quote: This approach would require the commissioning of the repeatedly abandoned Kosovo C project because it is still favored politically and included in national plans – despite increasingly well-founded doubts that this project could actually re-secure financing (Balkan Green Energy News, 2020).
